main.title: Leisure Suit Larry in the Land of the Lounge Lizards
main.subtitle: Leisure Suit Larry Turns Embarrassment into an Adventure-Game Mechanic
main.summary: On June 4, 1987 Sierra released Al Lowe's adventure built around Larry Laffer, a protagonist deliberately ill-equipped for the world he wants to conquer.

cards.heading: Leisure Suit Larry Turns Embarrassment into an Adventure-Game Mechanic
cards.text: Sierra released Al Lowe's Leisure Suit Larry in the Land of the Lounge Lizards on June 4, 1987. The adventure follows Larry Laffer's attempts to find romance in Lost Wages. Typed commands, puzzles and adult comedy repeatedly expose the gap between his ambitions and his abilities. Failed attempts often become part of the joke.

cards.heading: Larry Laffer arrives in Lost Wages
cards.text: The game's story follows its player character of a middle-aged male virgin named Larry Laffer as he desperately tries to "get lucky" in the fictional American city of Lost Wages. Land of the Lounge Lizards establishes several elements which recur in the later Leisure Suit Larry games, including Larry's campy attire, perpetual bad luck with women, and penchant for double-entendres. The game's overall plot and basic structure follow that of Softporn Adventure, Sierra's own 1981 Apple II text adventure that did not feature Larry.

cards.heading: Walking and typing commands
cards.text: Players control Larry's movements with the directional keys and by inputting commands into a text parser (e.g. "talk to man", "open window", etc.). If Larry is too far away from a person or object to comply, or if the command is invalid, a caution message appears with hints on what to do.

cards.heading: Taxis, money and the casino
cards.text: The game begins outside a bar in Lost Wages. The city consists of five areas: Lefty's Bar, a hotel-casino, a 24-hour wedding chapel, a disco, and a convenience store. The player can walk between areas that are next to each other, but other areas can only be accessed by hailing a taxi, which costs the player money; failure to do so results in Larry's being mugged or hit by oncoming traffic. To this end, money is essential to advance through the game. The only available method of augmenting Larry's funds is to gamble in the casino, playing blackjack and slots.

main.title: Ys I
main.summary: Ys I, originally known as Ys and titled on-screen Ancient Ys Vanished: Omen, is a 1987 action role-playing game developed by Nihon Falcom.

cards.text: Ys I, originally known as Ys and titled on-screen Ancient Ys Vanished: Omen, is a 1987 action role-playing game developed by Nihon Falcom. It is the first installment in the Ys series. Initially developed for the PC-88 by Masaya Hashimoto (director, programmer, designer) and Tomoyoshi Miyazaki (scenario writer), the game was soon ported to the Sharp X1, PC-98, FM-7, and MSX2 Japanese computer systems.

Set in a land called Esteria, the story centers around the titular civilization called Ys, which had mysteriously vanished 700 years ago with only traces of its existence being kept within the game's six books. When it is prophesied that an impeding darkness would come to threaten Esteria, a young and adventurous warrior named Adol Christin is called forward to collect these six books to aid him in vanquishing the darkness.

Ys I saw many subsequent releases, such as an English-language version for the Master System and an enhanced remake for the TurboGrafx-CD system as part of a compilation called Ys I & II, alongside its 1988 sequel Ys II: Ancient Ys Vanished – The Final Chapter. It was also adapted into an OVA series Ys. DotEmu has released the game on Android with the following localizations: English, French, Japanese, Korean, Russian, Italian, German, and Portuguese. A Nintendo Switch port of the game, based on the original PC-8800 release, was released in February 2024, 37 years after the game's initial release.

main.title: Bases Loaded
main.summary: Bases Loaded is a baseball video game originally developed by Tose and published by Jaleco for the Nintendo Entertainment System.

cards.text: Bases Loaded is a baseball video game originally developed by Tose and published by Jaleco for the Nintendo Entertainment System. It was first released in 1987 in Japan and in 1988 in North America, and a Game Boy port was released in July of 1990. For the Virtual Console, Bases Loaded was released on September 11, 2007, in Japan and on April 7, 2008, in North America for the Wii, and on May 15, 2013, in Japan and on July 10, 2014, in North America for Nintendo 3DS. The Wii U version in North America (which later released in Japan on October 22, 2014) was also released at the same time as the Nintendo 3DS version. A port by Mebius and Clarice Games for the PlayStation 4 was released in Japan in 2015.

The game is the first installment in the Bases Loaded series, followed by seven sequels across three generations of consoles. There are three more video games in the Bases Loaded NES series, Bases Loaded II: Second Season, Bases Loaded 3 and Bases Loaded 4. There was also a Game Boy version of Bases Loaded. The series continued onto the SNES platform with Super Bases Loaded, Super Bases Loaded 2, and Super Bases Loaded 3. The final entry to the series was Bases Loaded '96: Double Header, released for the Sega Saturn and PlayStation.

Bases Loaded is also the first in a series of sports games by Jaleco known in Japan as Moero!!. Baseball games were localized in the Western markets as the Bases Loaded series while the basketball game was localized as Hoops, the tennis game as Racket Attack and the soccer game as Goal!. Two titles went unlocalized: a baseball game Shin Moero!! Pro Yakyū and a judo game Moero!! Juudou Warriors.

main.title: Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic
main.subtitle: Doki Doki Panic Shows How a Game Can Change Identity Without Losing Its Rules
main.summary: On July 10, 1987 Fuji TV released Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic, developed by Nintendo for the Famicom Disk System.

cards.heading: Doki Doki Panic Shows How a Game Can Change Identity Without Losing Its Rules
cards.text: Fuji TV released Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic on July 10, 1987, developed by Nintendo for the Famicom Disk System. The platformer promoted the Yume Kōjō '87 event through four protagonists with different abilities. Players pull objects from the ground and lift or throw enemies. Nintendo later adapted these rules and levels into the international Super Mario Bros. 2, replacing the original cast with Mario characters.

cards.heading: Imajin, Lina, Mama and Papa
cards.text: The title Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic is derived from "doki doki", a Japanese onomatopoeia for the sound of a quickly beating heart. The title and character concept were inspired by a license cooperation between Nintendo and Fuji Television to promote the broadcaster's Yume Kōjō '87 event, which showcased several of its latest TV shows and consumer products. The Yume Kōjō festival's mascots became the game's protagonists: a family consisting of the boy Imajin, his girlfriend Lina, and his parents Mama and Papa. The rest of the game's characters, including the main villain named Mamu, were created by Nintendo for the project. Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic takes place within a book with an Arabian setting. All four characters are optionally playable, though the game is not fully completed until the player clears all levels using each protagonist.

cards.heading: A prototype about lifting, carrying and throwing
cards.text: The conception of a third Super Mario installment began shortly after the release of The Legend of Zelda in February 1986. An early prototype with vertical scrolling was developed in two months by Kensuke Tanabe, designed by a team led by Shigeru Miyamoto, and programmed by Nintendo's frequent partner, SRD. The first prototype's gameplay emphasizes vertically scrolling levels with two-player cooperative action: lifting, carrying, and throwing each other; lifting, carrying, throwing, stacking, and climbing objects; and incrementally scrolling the screen upward when reaching the top. Dissatisfied so far, Miyamoto then added the traditional horizontal scrolling, saying to "make something a little bit more Mario-like", and saying "Maybe we need to change this up ... As long as it's fun, anything goes". The prototype software was too complex for Famicom hardware at the time, and the gameplay was still considered lacking, especially in single-player mode.

cards.heading: How Nintendo converted Doki Doki Panic into Mario
cards.text: Nintendo rebuilt Doki Doki Panic's four protagonists as Mario, Luigi, Princess Toadstool and Toad for the international Super Mario Bros. 2. Their different abilities survived the change, with Luigi's scuttling legs explaining his higher jump. Several elements already fitted Mario's world, including POW blocks, invincibility stars, warp zones and Koji Kondo's music. The conversion also reduced repetition: players no longer had to finish every stage with every character. They could complete one run using any combination of the four, with a new B-button run adding another familiar Mario action.

main.title: Metal Gear
main.summary: Metal Gear is a 1987 action-adventure stealth game developed and published by Konami for the MSX2.

cards.heading: Metal Gear
cards.text: Metal Gear is a 1987 action-adventure stealth game developed and published by Konami for the MSX2. Originally released in Japan and parts of Europe in July 1987, it is the first game in the Metal Gear series and the first video game developed by Hideo Kojima. Players control Solid Snake, an operative of the U.S. special forces unit FOXHOUND, who is sent on a solo infiltration mission into the fortified state of Outer Heaven to destroy Metal Gear, a bipedal mecha capable of launching nuclear missiles to anywhere in the world, as well as rescue a number of fellow agents who have been taken hostage by the enemy.

cards.heading: Evasion instead of direct combat
cards.text: Initially envisioned as a pure action game, Metal Gear was reworked under Kojima to focus on avoiding enemies, contrary to the then-popular shoot 'em up genre, with an emphasis on evasion similar to Pac-Man (1980). Numerous weapons and items are used in the game, including a portable radio transceiver used to convey dialogue and the narrative. A port of the game was later released internationally for the Famicom/NES; this version was developed without Kojima's involvement and features many changes, including drastically altered level designs.

cards.heading: The design
cards.text: The MSX2 version of Metal Gear was released to positive reception, with praise directed towards the gameplay and graphics, while the Famicom/NES version received mixed reviews. The game was a commercial success, with the MSX2 version being a best-seller and the NES version selling 1 million units in the United States. Metal Gear is retrospectively recognized as the first mainstream stealth game, and is credited as a pioneer in stealth mechanics and complex storytelling via the radio transceiver. A direct sequel made by Kojima, Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake, and a sequel to the NES port, Snake's Revenge, were released in 1990. The MSX2 version was ported with a revised translation and additional gameplay features in Metal Gear Solid 3: Subsistence (2005), and this version was re-released along with the NES version as part of the Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 1 (2023).

main.title: Street Fighter
main.subtitle: Before the Perfect Combo There Was a Noisy Experiment
main.summary: Street Fighter is a 1987 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades.

cards.heading: Before the Perfect Combo There Was a Noisy Experiment
cards.text: Capcom's Street Fighter reached Japanese arcades on August 30, 1987. Ryu and Ken fight one-on-one using ordinary attacks and special moves entered through joystick sequences. Early cabinets tested large pressure-sensitive buttons before a six-button arrangement became the practical alternative. The game introduced characters and moves that its sequel would develop into a much larger fighting system.

cards.heading: The First Experiment Tries to Measure the Strength of a Hit
cards.text: One early cabinet configuration measured how hard players struck large pressure-sensitive buttons to determine the strength of a punch or kick. The arrangement proved impractical and was replaced with six buttons for light, medium and heavy attacks. Players could then select strength directly through a separate button, making the controls more predictable.

cards.heading: Two Nearly Identical Fighters Create a Space for Human Comparison
cards.text: The first player controls Ryu, while a second can join as Ken. They share most of their moves, so the duel largely depends on how the two players handle the same tools. Timing an attack, judging its range and choosing when to risk a special move can make the difference. Street Fighter II would later broaden the selectable cast substantially.

cards.heading: Hadoken and Shoryuken Turn an Input Sequence into Knowledge
cards.text: Hadoken, Shoryuken and Tatsumaki Senpukyaku require sequences of directions followed by an attack button. Discovering the command is only the beginning: players must perform it reliably during a fight. The first game's strict inputs make this difficult, but the special moves already provide a layer of practice beyond the normal punches and kicks.

main.title: Digital Devil Story: Megami Tensei
main.subtitle: The Monster Can Change Sides
main.summary: On September 11, 1987, Namco released Digital Devil Story: Megami Tensei for Famicom in Japan, developed by Atlus from the universe of Aya Nishitani's novels.

cards.heading: The Monster Can Change Sides
cards.text: Namco released Atlus's Digital Devil Story: Megami Tensei for the Famicom in Japan on September 11, 1987. Based on the universe of Aya Nishitani's novels, it is a first-person dungeon RPG. Demons encountered in its corridors can be fought, recruited through negotiation and fused into other creatures. These systems became central to later Megami Tensei and Shin Megami Tensei games.

cards.heading: The Map Forms First in the Player's Mind
cards.text: First-person corridors reveal only a small part of each labyrinth. Players must remember turns, stairs and doors, often using notes to maintain a route. A wrong turn can consume supplies before the next fight, while learning a shortcut makes a return trip less costly. Exploration depends on knowing both where to go and how much the party can spend getting there.

cards.heading: Talking Changes the Meaning of an Encounter
cards.text: An encounter can lead to conversation as well as combat. Persuading a demon to join adds its abilities to the party, giving players a reason to consider creatures they might otherwise defeat. The developers drew on their interest in tabletop role-playing and the possibility of talking to an apparent enemy. Recruitment makes learning the bestiary useful beyond identifying threats.

cards.heading: The Party Also Grows by Giving Up What It Has
cards.text: Fusion exchanges existing demons for a new creature. The player gives up abilities currently available in order to build a party suited to later challenges. Recruiting another demon can therefore matter both for immediate combat and for the combinations it makes possible. Deciding when to keep an ally and when to fuse it becomes a recurring part of progression.

main.title: Maniac Mansion
main.summary: Maniac Mansion is a 1987 graphic adventure video game developed and published by Lucasfilm Games.

cards.heading: Maniac Mansion
cards.text: Maniac Mansion is a 1987 graphic adventure video game developed and published by Lucasfilm Games. It follows teenage protagonist Dave Miller as he attempts to rescue his girlfriend Sandy Pantz from a mad scientist, whose mind has been enslaved by a sentient meteor. The player uses a point-and-click interface to guide Dave and two of his six playable friends through the scientist's mansion while solving puzzles and avoiding dangers. Gameplay is non-linear, and the game must be completed in different ways based on the player's choice of characters. Initially released for the Commodore 64 and Apple II, Maniac Mansion was Lucasfilm Games' first self-published product.

cards.heading: Paper plans and the SCUMM engine
cards.text: The game was conceived in 1985 by Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick, who sought to tell a comedic story based on horror film and B-movie clichés. They mapped out the project as a paper-and-pencil game before coding commenced. While earlier adventure titles had relied on command lines, Gilbert disliked such systems, and he developed Maniac Mansion's simpler point-and-click interface as a replacement. To speed up production, he created a game engine called SCUMM, which was used in many later LucasArts titles. After its release, Maniac Mansion was ported to several platforms. A port for the Nintendo Entertainment System had to be reworked heavily, in response to Nintendo of America's concerns that the game was inappropriate for children.

cards.heading: Maniac Mansion
cards.text: Maniac Mansion was critically acclaimed: reviewers lauded its graphics, cutscenes, animation, and humor. Writer Orson Scott Card praised it as a step toward "computer games [becoming] a valid storytelling art". It influenced numerous graphic adventure titles, and its point-and-click interface became a standard feature in the genre. The game's success solidified Lucasfilm as a serious rival to adventure game studios such as Sierra On-Line. In 1990, Maniac Mansion was adapted into a three-season television series of the same name, written by Eugene Levy and starring Joe Flaherty. A sequel to the game, Day of the Tentacle, was released in 1993.

main.title: Faxanadu
main.subtitle: A troubled homecoming
main.summary: Faxanadu is a side-scrolling action role-playing game developed by Hudson Soft for the NES. A traveller returns to Eolis to find an almost deserted town: its water supply has failed and hostile dwarves threaten the elves. The king sends him out with a little gold and a large problem. Towns, passages and dungeons form a connected journey in which the next purchase can matter as much as the next sword fight. The name joins Famicom and Xanadu, although Hudson built a distinct adventure around Falcom’s licence.

cards.heading: A troubled homecoming
cards.text: Faxanadu is a side-scrolling action role-playing game developed by Hudson Soft for the NES. A traveller returns to Eolis to find an almost deserted town: its water supply has failed and hostile dwarves threaten the elves. The king sends him out with a little gold and a large problem. Towns, passages and dungeons form a connected journey in which the next purchase can matter as much as the next sword fight. The name joins Famicom and Xanadu, although Hudson built a distinct adventure around Falcom’s licence.

cards.heading: Between towns and monsters
cards.text: The hero walks, jumps and climbs through spaces occupied by enemies, ladders and narrow platforms. A sword handles nearby threats while magic provides a way to strike from a distance. Defeated creatures can leave money or bread, linking survival to the economy of the journey. Shops sell equipment and useful supplies, so returning to a settlement gives exploration a practical rhythm. Each departure asks the player to judge whether the current weapon, armour and remaining resources are enough for the route ahead.

cards.heading: A journey worth recording
cards.text: Progress also has a place in the world. Gurus offer passwords called mantras, allowing the adventure to continue later without a battery save. Experience raises the hero’s rank, while money and equipment provide more immediate improvements. These systems give the journey two scales: the individual jump or encounter and the longer preparation for an unfamiliar area. Faxanadu’s appeal lies in that combination. Reaching a town feels like an arrival because the road has demanded attention, and leaving it means carrying a new set of possibilities.

main.title: Wizards & Warriors
main.subtitle: Rare · Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Wizards & Warriors is Rare's NES action platformer about Kuros, a knight travelling through the kingdom of Elrond to rescue a princess from the wizard Malkil. Forests, caves and the rooms of Castle IronSpire contain treasure, enemies and magical equipment. The journey encourages searching above and below the obvious route, with branches and platforms offering access to further discoveries. Kuros carries a sword, but his prospects also depend on the useful objects collected while exploring the surroundings of each stage.

cards.heading: A knight searching the forest
cards.text: Wizards & Warriors is Rare's NES action platformer about Kuros, a knight travelling through the kingdom of Elrond to rescue a princess from the wizard Malkil. Forests, caves and the rooms of Castle IronSpire contain treasure, enemies and magical equipment. The journey encourages searching above and below the obvious route, with branches and platforms offering access to further discoveries. Kuros carries a sword, but his prospects also depend on the useful objects collected while exploring the surroundings of each stage.

cards.heading: Treasure pays for the passage
cards.text: Gems are needed to satisfy the guardian blocking progress, giving exploration a purpose beyond improving the score. Colour-coded keys open matching doors and chests, while weapons and magical objects change what Kuros can do. A returning projectile provides another way to strike enemies, and special equipment helps with dangerous terrain or difficult jumps. The player repeatedly balances searching with the need to stay alive. Health falls through injury and the passage of time, making food another important discovery along the route.

cards.heading: Keep the discoveries, try again
cards.text: Continuing after losing all lives preserves collected equipment while resetting the score. That choice keeps a failed attempt connected to the discoveries already made, helping an unfamiliar maze become manageable over successive tries. David Wise composed the music for a game released early in Rare's NES career, after Slalom. Acclaim published it in North America, beginning a series that continued with Ironsword and further sequels. Its mixture of platforming and treasure hunting makes a forest feel like a collection of places worth investigating.
